# Loading Your Data

Having measured our reflexes, we now have to load those data into this script:

```{r}
# In this case, floats have been written using comma (,). Thus, we 
# inform read.csv() that we want something else as a column separator
# (anything would work in this case, besides comma).
data <- read.csv('reflexes.csv', sep = ' ')
# head() returns the first six rows of the data frame
head(data)
```

Now, to compute the mean value of times, we can just first make our times a vector:

```{r}
times <- data$X2.984
mean(times)
```

This does not run saying that our data are not numeric?

To check the type of our loaded data, we can use this:

```{r}
str(data)
```

Indeed, R has treated everything as characters! To resolve this:

```{r}
times <- as.numeric(data$X2.984)
mean(times)
```

Now, everything is NA! This is due to us using commas instead of dots, so we have to first fix all this:

```{r}
times <- sub(',', '.', data$X2.984)
str(times)
```

Now, we can parse them as floats:

```{r}
times <- as.numeric(times)
mean(times)
```

But, is the mean value good enough? Let us plots a histogram to see the underlying distribution:

```{r}
hist(times)
```

Ideally, we should take into account extremes values that cancel, so we can measure distance from 3 instead of just reaction time:

```{r}
dist <- abs(times - 3)
mean(dist)
```

Also, the corresponding histogram:

```{r}
hist(dist)
```

But, means might deceive you, especially in the presence of extreme values, so we also compute the median:

```{r}
median(dist)
```

We might also consider the sample's range:

```{r}
dist_range <- range(dist)
dist_range
dist_range_R <- dist_range[2] - dist_range[1]
print(dist_range_R)
```

Also, to compute our standard deviation:

```{r}
var(dist)
sd(dist)
```
